question: Which treatment works best for this one patient?

hawksworth2024.cite: Hawksworth et al. (2024). A methodological review of randomised n-of-1 trials. Trials 25: 263.

steps.title: One patient
steps.text: The question is about one person, not the average patient: of two treatments, which helps them?

quotes.text: n-of-1 trials are within-patient, multi-period crossover trials designed to optimise the evaluation of health technologies in individual patients

steps.title: Randomise periods
steps.text: Treatment periods come in pairs, one of each treatment; chance decides the order inside each pair.

quotes.text: In these trials, a single patient receives one treatment for a period of time and then switches to receive another.
Usually, the order in which the patient receives the treatments is randomised.

steps.title: Blind
steps.text: Where possible, the treatments look the same, so the patient's hopes cannot colour the score.

quotes.text: The majority of studies blinded participants to treatment allocation (n = 57, 77.0%).

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Switch back and forth several times and measure in every period. One good week can be luck; the same winner pair after pair is not.

quotes.text: This “switching” is repeated, such that multiple measurements are obtained for each treatment.
The median (Q1, Q3) number of periods was six (4, 8). The median (Q1, Q3) period length was 14 days (5, 28).

steps.title: Decide
steps.text: The result answers the question for this patient: keep the treatment that won.

quotes.text: Such n-of-1 trials combine methodological rigour with the investigation of treatment effects in an individual patient to enable the determination of the optimal treatment for a particular patient, enabling individualised patient care

carryover.text: the effect of the first intervention persists into the second period so that the observed difference between the treatments depends on the order in which they were received
carryover.where: Methodological features of randomised crossover trials

limits: The card's defining paper, Guyatt et al. The quotes come from Hawksworth et al. (2024) instead.
The order of periods and the symptom scores in the pictures are made up to show the idea; they are not from a real trial.
No exercise: the pictures carry the idea.
